keep: Goodyear called it application. Parton called it an accident, and the accident is the version that stuck.
lede: He spent ten years in and out of debtors' prisons, melted his first pound of rubber while confined to the jail limits, and refused to call his discovery an accident. Most retellings since have called it one.
copy: Charles Goodyear's family hardware firm failed around 1830, owing thirty thousand dollars. For ten years after, in his own words, he "was repeatedly imprisoned for debt". He took up India rubber in 1834, while confined to the limits of a jail. Rubber then was a fashion with a flaw: his own compound decomposed in a batch of mail-bags. In 1838, at Woburn, Massachusetts, he bought Nathaniel Hayward's claim for mixing sulphur into it, patented in February 1839. The claim, Goodyear wrote, "was for the use of sulphur, and not for the heating or vulcanizing process, subsequently discovered by the writer."

That winter, at Woburn, a specimen of the sulphur compound, "being carelessly brought in contact with a hot stove, charred like leather". In later trials before an open fire, the edge of the charred part showed a border "not charred, but perfectly cured". He would not call it luck, though he allowed that the Creator aids his creatures "by what are termed accidents". The discovery, he wrote, was not "what is commonly termed accident" but "the result of the closest application and observation". It took him five more years. On 21 April 1840 he wrote from the debtors' prison in Boston that it was "perhaps as good a resting place as any this side the grave." US patent 3,633, of 15 June 1844, mixed twenty-five parts of rubber with five of sulphur and seven of white lead, heated close to 270 degrees. In London, Thomas Hancock had been handed a few bits of the American rubber in the autumn of 1842. His own British patent passed the great seal on 21 November 1843.

Whether the patent ever paid him is doubtful. In Goodyear v. Day, in 1852, Daniel Webster argued his case, paid by the companies licensed under it. The proofs ran to about 4,000 printed pages. The court held that no one had made the thing before him. James Parton reported in 1867 that the licensees paid Webster $25,000, and doubted that Goodyear ever cleared as much from his patents. At the Paris Exposition of 1855 he was in Clichy, the debtors' prison, when his son brought him the Legion of Honour. He died at the Fifth Avenue Hotel in New York in 1860, on his way to his daughter's funeral. He died insolvent, Parton wrote, "leaving to a wife and six children only an inheritance of debt." The Goodyear Tire & Rubber Company traces its origins to 1898, when Frank Seiberling bought two empty factories in Akron; its own history says he was inspired by Goodyear.

bio.t: Noble Obsession: Charles Goodyear, Thomas Hancock, and the Race to Unlock the Greatest Industrial Secret of the Nineteenth Century
bio.why: Its subtitle sets the story as a race with Thomas Hancock, which the record bears out. Read Goodyear's own Gum-Elastic and Its Varieties (1853) for the stove in his words, and James Parton's chapter of 1867 to see where the accident came from.

contested: Who got there first, and the numbers that grew. Thomas Hancock's Personal Narrative (1857) never names Goodyear. He says he made no analysis of the American samples and worked "entirely and solely" on his own, and he also concedes that they "showed me for the first time that the desirable change in the condition of rubber of not stiffening by cold had been attained". His British patent was sealed seven months before Goodyear's American one. It was his associate Brockedon, by Hancock's account, who proposed the word vulcanisation. The stove grew in the retelling: Goodyear's careless contact became, in Parton, "a violent gesture" in mid-argument, and later a spill in the kitchen. Wikipedia credits Goodyear with US patent 1,090 of 1839; Finkelstein and Rovetti's history for Connecticut Humanities shows it was Hayward's sulphur patent, which Goodyear bought. The numbers: no source opened here counts his imprisonments (Parton says he was "seldom out of jail a whole year from 1835 to 1841"); American Heritage puts Webster's fee at $15,000 against Parton's $25,000; and the $200,000 of debt at his death that circulates is in neither Parton nor Bradford Peirce's life of 1866, which say only that he died insolvent.
